title: Burns
summary: Thermal, chemical and electrical burns: stop the burning, cool with running water, estimate size, cover loosely, and decide on evacuation.

steps.text: Make sure the scene is safe and stop the burning. Get the person away from the heat source if you can do it safely.
steps.detail:
Your safety first: do not become a second casualty. Move the person away from flames, hot surfaces or hot liquid if it is safe to do so. If it is safe, move them to clean running water.

Electrical injury: do not touch the person until you are sure the power is off.

Chemical burn: protect yourself with gloves and eye protection if you have them, and do not spread the chemical onto yourself, others, or unburned skin.

Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Is it a chemical burn (acid, lye, cleaner, fuel or other chemical)?
Is it an electrical burn (electric shock or lightning)?
Remove rings, watches, belts and tight clothing from the burned area now, before it swells. Leave anything that is stuck to the skin.
steps.detail: Burned areas swell, and jewellery or tight clothing can then cut off circulation (AHA). Remove clothing near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin (Red Cross).

steps.text: Cool the burn under clean, cool running water right away, for 5 to 20 minutes (electrical burns: at least 15). Watch children for shivering.
steps.detail:
Cool thermal burns immediately, preferably with clean running water (AHA, Class 1). Cooling for 5 to 20 minutes may be reasonable (AHA); Red Cross also says 5 to 20 minutes. There is no agreed best duration. For an electrical burn, Red Cross says cool for at least 15 minutes.

Water temperature: cool or cold clean running water (AHA, Red Cross). If you have no cool water, lukewarm water is acceptable (Red Cross).

No running water: use a cool or cold compress, such as a clean cloth soaked in cool water (Red Cross). AHA (2024) also allows ice wrapped in a cloth, for no more than 10 minutes, but only on a superficial burn where the skin is not broken; Red Cross says do not use ice.

Watch for getting cold: children (before their teens) cool down fast and can become hypothermic while a burn is cooled, so watch them for shivering or feeling cold (AHA). AHA and Red Cross say to monitor for hypothermia but give no rule for when to stop. A reasonable judgement, not from a source: if a child starts shivering, stop cooling, dry and cover them, and keep them warm. With a large burn, watch any casualty for hypothermia (Red Cross, WMS). Cool the burn, not the whole person, and keep the rest of them covered and warm.

Do not try to clean a severe burn (Red Cross).
steps.warn: No ice on blistered, broken or deep burns. Keep the rest of the body warm, especially children.

steps.text: Estimate the burn size: count only blistered or deeper burns, not skin that is just red. Their whole hand (palm and fingers) is about 1%.
steps.detail:
Burn depth (AHA, Red Cross):
- Superficial: red and painful, no blisters, only the outer layer of skin. Usually heals without a scar.
- Partial-thickness: blisters, which may ooze; the outer and second layers of skin are damaged.
- Full-thickness: through all the skin and possibly into fat, muscle or bone. The skin may look white, brown, black or charred, and there may be little or no pain.
Any burn deeper than superficial needs medical care (Red Cross).

Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns count towards the size; skin that is only red is left out (StatPearls; NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation).

Use the burn area tool: tap each body region that is burned. For small or scattered burns, count how many of the casualty's own whole hands (palm and fingers together) would cover them: each is about 1% of their body. The palm alone, without fingers, is about 0.5%.

Field estimates are rough. TCCC estimates to the nearest 10% using the rule of nines.

steps.text: Decide on evacuation using the list: deep burns, blistered burns bigger than their palm, burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, or smoke breathed in.
steps.detail:
Get medical care (AHA): any full-thickness burn; a partial-thickness (blistered) burn larger than the casualty's palm; a partial-thickness burn on the face, hands, feet or genitals.

Get help urgently for signs that hot smoke or gases were breathed in: burns to the face, singed nose hairs, soot around the nose or mouth, or difficulty breathing (AHA). TCCC: facial burns, especially from a fire in an enclosed space, may come with injury to the airway, so watch breathing closely.

Burns on the face, hands, feet or genitals, or over more than 10% of the body (5% in a child), are usually treated in a burn centre (AHA). Large burns can cause major fluid loss and organ failure.

Red Cross also lists: burns all the way around an arm, leg, the chest or the neck; electrical, chemical, radiation or explosion burns; burns in a young child, an older person, or someone with other injuries or medical conditions; and any burn on a child.

Off-grid (WMS): also evacuate burns that become infected or whose pain you cannot control.

The full list is under When to evacuate, and the burn area tool shows it beside the total.

steps.text: Cover the burn loosely with a clean, dry, non-stick dressing or clean cloth. No butter, grease, oils or adhesive bandages on it.
steps.detail:
Cover burned skin and intact blisters loosely with a clean cloth or a non-stick dry dressing (AHA, Red Cross, TCCC). This protects the burn, eases pain, and does not trap heat. Do not use adhesive bandages on the burn (Red Cross).

Chemical and electrical burns: Red Cross leaves them uncovered while waiting for EMS, and covers them loosely if EMS is delayed or the person has to be moved. Off-grid that usually means covering them loosely.

Do not put butter, mayonnaise, petroleum jelly or other greasy substances on a burn: they trap heat (Red Cross).

Later, for a small partial-thickness burn you are looking after yourself (not one that needs evacuation), AHA says petroleum jelly, an antibiotic ointment in petroleum jelly, honey, or aloe vera under a clean non-stick dressing may be reasonable, after the burn has been cooled. Red Cross says not to put petroleum jelly on a burn.

Large burns: TCCC wraps a casualty with burns over 20% of the body in an emergency blanket or heat-reflective shell, which covers the burns and helps prevent hypothermia.

steps.text: Keep them warm, watch their breathing, and treat for shock if the burn is large. For a small burn, over-the-counter pain medicine is reasonable (see warning).
steps.warn: No pain medicine by mouth if there are signs of shock, the burn needs evacuation, a head injury is possible, or they are less alert than normal.
steps.detail:
Burn casualties lose heat quickly: keep them covered and off cold ground (TCCC, Red Cross).

Watch breathing closely after a burn to the face or a fire in an enclosed space; it can get worse (TCCC, AHA).

Large burns can cause shock: use the Shock protocol and evacuate urgently.

Pain: over-the-counter acetaminophen or ibuprofen-type medicine is reasonable for burn pain (AHA), taken as the package directs. Do not give it when the Shock protocol applies (nothing by mouth), for a burn large or serious enough to need evacuation, or when a head injury is possible or they are less alert than normal: Red Cross advises against painkillers after a head injury because they can hide the signs of a serious injury.

Keep checking the burn for signs of infection while you wait or travel: spreading redness, swelling, pus, worse pain, or fever.

steps.text: Brush off any dry chemical, then flush with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing and jewellery.
steps.detail:
Get the chemical off the skin straight away (AHA). Flush the skin with running water for at least 15 minutes, unless the chemical's own instructions or a poison centre say otherwise (AHA, Red Cross).

Dry chemicals: brush off as much as you can first, with a gloved hand or a cloth, without spreading it (AHA, Red Cross). Some dry chemicals (for example lye powder, or sodium or potassium metal) react with water.

Remove contaminated clothing, jewellery and anything else touching the area so the chemical is not held against the skin (AHA).

Some chemicals, such as hydrofluoric acid and phenol, need special treatment other than water; follow the product label, safety data sheet, or a poison centre if you can reach one.

Call for help (EMS) for a large exposure, breathing problems, or if the person feels unwell all over (AHA).

steps.text: Did the chemical also get into an eye?

ask.q: Did the chemical get into an eye?

steps.text: Electrical: make sure the power is off before you touch them. Check breathing; be ready to give CPR.
steps.detail:
Electricity can stop the heart and breathing (Red Cross). Do not touch the person until the power source is off.

Every electrical burn needs to be checked by a health care provider, even a small one, because the injury inside can be much worse than the skin shows (Red Cross).

steps.text: Not breathing normally: start CPR now. Use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant), and an AED if you have one.
steps.detail: Red Cross: be ready to give CPR and use an AED after an electrical injury. Treat the burns once breathing and circulation are dealt with.

steps.text: Chemical in the eye: use the Eye injury protocol now and flush the eye for 15 minutes. Treat the skin burn afterwards.
steps.detail:
Flush the eye immediately with plenty of clean water (AHA). Red Cross: keep flushing the eye until help takes over. The Eye injury protocol has the steps.

After the eye has been flushed, come back to this protocol for the burn size and dressing.

donts: Do not put ice on a blistered, broken or deep burn, or leave wrapped ice on any burn for more than 10 minutes.
Do not put butter, mayonnaise, grease, oil or petroleum jelly on a fresh burn.
Do not use adhesive bandages on a burn.
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the burn.
Do not try to clean a severe burn.
Do not touch someone after an electric shock until the power is off.
Do not let a child or someone with a large burn get cold while you cool the burn.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently: signs of breathing in smoke or hot gases (burns to the face, singed nose hairs, soot around nose or mouth, difficulty breathing).
Evacuate urgently: burns over 10% of the body in an adult or 5% in a child (usually treated in a burn centre). Over 20%: needs IV fluids (TCCC); go as fast as possible and keep them warm.
Evacuate urgently: a burn that goes all the way around an arm, leg, the chest or the neck.
Get medical care: any full-thickness burn (white, brown, black or charred, little pain), or a blistered burn larger than the casualty's palm.
Get medical care: burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals or a joint.
Get medical care: every electrical, lightning, chemical, radiation or explosion burn, even a small one.
Get medical care: any burn on a child, an older person, or someone with other injuries or illnesses.
Off-grid: also evacuate a burn that becomes infected or pain you cannot control (WMS).
notes: Count only blistered (partial-thickness) and deeper (full-thickness: white, brown, black or leathery, often little pain) burns. Leave out skin that is only red.
Small or scattered burns: the casualty's whole hand, palm and fingers together, is about 1% of their body.

The child figure shows a baby's proportions (age 0). For every year of age, take 1% from the head and add 0.5% to each leg (NSW ACI); for example at age 5, head 13% and each leg 16.5%. From age 9, use the adult figure.
Field estimates are rough. TCCC rounds to the nearest 10%.
